strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: using one sparse-view CT reconstruction model across acquisition rates and spatial resolutions. The combination of sinogram- and image-domain processing is well motivated by CT physics.

The sinogram design has useful inductive biases, including flipped circular padding for parallel-beam angular periodicity and detector-axis Fourier processing motivated by the Fourier slice theorem and filtered backprojection.

Results on two anatomical datasets are consistently strong. CTO substantially improves PSNR, RMSE, and SSIM over the reported CNN, transformer, iterative, and diffusion baselines, while inference is much faster than iterative diffusion reconstruction.

The paper includes several relevant analyses: spatial- versus frequency-domain processing, alternative Fourier axes, angular-boundary padding, full-test-set results, multiple view counts, and qualitative comparisons. The presentation is generally clear and the supplementary material provides useful implementation details.
weaknesses: The central multi-rate generalization claim is not convincingly tested. The main experiment trains a single model jointly on every evaluated view count, so it demonstrates multi-rate fitting rather than generalization to unseen sampling rates or patterns. Evaluation on held-out view counts, nonuniform masks, angular offsets, and limited-angle settings is needed.

The zero-shot image-resolution experiment uses bilinearly upsampled 512×512 ground truth rather than native high-resolution targets. It therefore mainly tests agreement with interpolation, not recovery of additional high-resolution anatomical information. The sinogram-resolution experiment similarly reports only a 72-to-144-view comparison against a CNN, without comparisons to interpolation, retraining, or other resolution-agnostic methods.

The key CTO-versus-CNN comparison does not isolate the claimed benefit of DISCO. The supplement says the CNN baseline operates entirely in image space, whereas CTO additionally contains two learned sinogram UDNO branches. This conflicts with the suggestion of an architecture-matched comparison; parameter counts, FLOPs, and a convolutional version of the complete CTO architecture are absent. Consequently, the large gain cannot be attributed specifically to function-space kernels.

The diffusion comparison is weak support for the state-of-the-art claim. The diffusion prior is reported as trained for only 2,000 iterations, the compared methods are generic posterior samplers rather than leading CT-specific models, and their 1,000-step configuration makes the speed advantage largely predetermined. Training convergence and tuning fairness are not documented.

All projections appear to be synthetically generated from already reconstructed images. There is no evaluation on raw measurements, realistic photon/electronic noise, scanner-domain shifts, or different geometries. This substantially limits the clinical-deployment claims.

The equivariance derivation applies to parallel-beam data with the pi-periodicity-with-flip identity, while the AAPM experiment uses fan-beam geometry over [0,2pi). The paper does not explain how the proposed boundary condition and equivariance argument change for fan-beam measurements. Moreover, the evaluation provides no quantitative equivariance error or rotated-test robustness; a padding ablation alone does not establish rotational equivariance of the entire multiscale network.

Important reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous, including the exact data-consistency update and initialization, complex-feature handling in the Fourier branch, parameter counts, training duration, per-baseline multi-rate training protocol, and number of AAPM test patients. There is also no code-availability statement.

Overall, this is a promising Algorithms/General submission with encouraging empirical results, but the experiments do not yet substantiate its headline resolution-independent and unseen-acquisition generalization claims. The confounded CNN comparison and geometry mismatch push the balance slightly toward rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: using one reconstruction model across multiple sparse-view rates and spatial discretizations. The combination of sinogram- and image-domain processing with explicit data-consistency updates is well motivated.

The sinogram boundary treatment incorporates the parallel-beam identity p(theta+pi,r)=p(theta,-r), providing a sensible physical inductive bias. Processing detector-axis Fourier coefficients is also reasonably connected to the Fourier-slice theorem and filtered backprojection.

Reported reconstruction results are consistently strong on two datasets. CTO substantially improves PSNR, RMSE, and SSIM over the evaluated learned baselines while requiring only 0.065 seconds per inference, according to the manuscript.

The paper is generally readable and includes useful supplementary details, large held-out test sets for the kidney experiments, qualitative comparisons, a padding ablation, and comparisons among several Fourier-processing variants.
weaknesses: The central multi-rate generalization claim is overstated. The main model is jointly trained on all evaluated sampling rates, so these experiments demonstrate multi-rate fitting rather than generalization to unseen acquisition rates. Only the limited 72-to-144-view experiment addresses an unseen rate, and no comprehensive unseen-rate or unseen-pattern evaluation is provided.

The cross-resolution evidence is not clinically or scientifically convincing. The image experiment trains at 256x256, bilinearly upsamples both the intermediate reconstruction and ground truth to 512x512, and evaluates against that interpolated target. This primarily tests consistency with interpolation, not recovery of genuine high-resolution anatomy. Only one resolution transition is evaluated, with no native high-resolution measurements or comparison to resolution-specific models.

The most important comparison does not isolate the proposed neural-operator design. The supplement describes the Unrolled CNN as an entirely image-domain model with no learned sinogram processing, whereas CTO includes spatial and frequency sinogram branches. This also conflicts with the main text's characterization of the baseline as replacing DISCO layers with regular convolutions. Consequently, the reported 3–4 dB advantage cannot be attributed to function-space kernels. A matched dual-domain CNN, parameter/FLOP counts, and component-wise ablations are required.

The rotation-equivariance claim exceeds what is established. The derivation covers an ideal stationary convolution under parallel-beam symmetry, but not the complete network containing discretization, pooling, nonlinearities, inverse Radon transforms, and data-consistency operations. The experiments provide only a padding ablation and qualitative examples at a few rotations, rather than equivariance error over arbitrary rotations. Moreover, the AAPM experiment uses fan-beam geometry, for which the stated parallel-beam pi-periodicity argument does not directly apply.

All projections are simulated from already reconstructed images, apparently without a realistic measurement-noise, calibration, or acquisition model. This substantially limits conclusions about dose reduction, scanner variability, clinical deployment, and generalization to real raw CT measurements. Evaluation is also limited to two datasets and fixed geometries.

Baseline credibility is insufficient. The 65-million-parameter diffusion model is reportedly trained for only 2,000 iterations, which is unlikely to yield a competitive image prior, while inference is deliberately run for 1,000 steps. The resulting quality and 500x speed claims therefore do not establish superiority over well-trained modern diffusion reconstruction systems. Hyperparameter selection and joint-rate training protocols are not consistently documented across learned baselines.

The implementation and evaluation details are inadequate for reliable reproduction: handling of complex FFT features, quadrature and coordinate normalization across resolutions, data-consistency parameters, preprocessing and PSNR data range, HU calibration, parameter counts, and patient-level uncertainty are missing or unclear. No code or pretrained-model availability is stated.

The novelty is moderate and largely compositional: DISCO/UDNO operators, unrolled reconstruction, dual-domain processing, and frequency-domain sinogram filtering are existing ideas. Given the confounded ablations and weak tests of the defining generalization claims, the manuscript does not yet supply enough evidence that their combination constitutes a convincingly validated Algorithms/General contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: using one sparse-view CT model across acquisition rates and spatial discretizations. The joint sinogram/image-domain formulation, physics-based data-consistency updates, detector-axis frequency processing, and geometry-aware padding form a coherent Algorithms/General contribution.

Results are strong and consistent across two patient-held-out datasets. CTO improves substantially over classical reconstruction, diffusion methods, DuDoTrans, GloReDi, and an unrolled CNN in RMSE, PSNR, and SSIM, including gains of roughly 3–6 dB over learned baselines in several settings.

The method is computationally attractive: reported inference takes 0.065 seconds on an A100, versus 32–52 seconds for the evaluated diffusion approaches. This materially strengthens its potential impact.

The paper motivates the sinogram-domain design using CT geometry and the Fourier-slice theorem. Ablations support detector-axis frequency processing and flipped circular padding, while qualitative examples show visibly reduced artifacts.

The presentation is generally clear, with useful architectural diagrams, implementation details, patient-level data separation, full-test-set results for non-diffusion methods, and supplementary derivations.
weaknesses: The central cross-rate generalization claim is overstated. The main multi-rate experiment trains jointly on every evaluated rate (9, 18, 36, and 72 views), demonstrating a useful multi-rate model but not generalization to unseen sparse-view rates. Only the 72-to-144-view experiment tests an unseen angular discretization, so claims such as working at “any sampling rate” need broader zero-shot evidence.

The image “super-resolution” experiment uses a 512×512 target obtained by bilinearly interpolating the 256×256 ground truth. It therefore evaluates discretization consistency on interpolated images, not recovery of genuine high-resolution anatomical information. Native high-resolution targets and several train/test resolution ratios are needed to substantiate the stronger claim.

The comparison to the unrolled CNN does not cleanly isolate the benefit of DISCO/function-space learning: the stated CNN baseline operates only in the image domain, whereas CTO additionally has learned spatial and frequency sinogram branches. A matched dual-domain CNN and component-wise ablations of NOs, NOi, and frequency processing are important.

The rotation-equivariance argument is derived for parallel-beam CT using the π-periodicity-with-flip identity, but AAPM experiments use fan-beam geometry over 2π. The paper does not explain whether the data are rebinned or how the padding/symmetry is modified for fan-beam measurements. Moreover, the evidence measures a padding-induced PSNR gain rather than numerical equivariance error over arbitrary rotations.

Baseline and reproducibility details leave concerns: the 65M-parameter diffusion prior is reportedly trained for only 2,000 iterations; CTO training duration, learned data-consistency parameters, normalization, and resolution-dependent quadrature details are missing; and the “no tuning required” claim conflicts with the explicitly hyperparameter-tuned DISCO basis. Experiments also use simulated sinograms without a documented realistic noise model, limiting the clinical/deployment conclusions.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: deploying one sparse-view CT reconstruction model across varying acquisition configurations. The function-space perspective is well motivated for this setting.

CTO combines sinogram- and image-domain processing, explicit data consistency, detector-axis frequency processing, and geometry-aware angular padding in a coherent architecture. Adapting DISCO operators to sinogram coordinates is a useful contribution, although most individual components build on prior work.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering AAPM, KiTS, and LIDC-IDRI data, multiple view counts, classical and learned baselines, ablations, runtime, parameter/FLOP comparisons, simulated noise, and cross-dataset transfer. Reported reconstruction gains are large and generally consistent across PSNR, SSIM, and HU RMSE.

The authors provide a matched-parameter CTO/CNN comparison in Table 11, where CTO retains an approximately 2 dB advantage, as well as ablations supporting the spatial and frequency sinogram branches. Inference is substantially faster than the evaluated iterative diffusion approaches.
The manuscript is generally clear, with helpful diagrams and qualitative comparisons, and the supplementary material supplies substantial implementation and complexity information.
weaknesses: The central multi-rate generalization claim is not convincingly evaluated. In the main experiment, one model is trained on exactly the same four view counts—9, 18, 36, and 72—used for testing. This demonstrates multi-task fitting to seen rates, not generalization to unseen sampling rates. Results on held-out intermediate rates, unseen masks or angular offsets, and harder extrapolation to fewer views are needed.

The image-resolution experiment does not establish genuine zero-shot super-resolution: both the 256×256 intermediate reconstruction and the ground truth are bilinearly enlarged to 512×512. The target therefore contains no additional high-resolution information. This mainly measures behavior under coordinate resampling and cannot substantiate claims about reconstructing at arbitrary physical image resolution.

The rotation-equivariance claim is overstated and partly inconsistent with the experimental geometry. The proof applies to a stationary sinogram convolution under the parallel-beam identity p(theta+pi,r)=p(theta,-r), whereas AAPM is explicitly simulated using fan-beam geometry. Moreover, equivariance of the sinogram module alone does not make the complete pipeline equivariant: the Cartesian image-space DISCO/UDNO is not shown to be SO(2)-equivariant. The padding PSNR ablation and three qualitative cardinal rotations do not measure equivariance error.

The key comparison to the Unrolled CNN is ambiguous. The main paper describes it as the same architecture with DISCO replaced by ordinary convolutions, but Supplement B.2 says it operates entirely in image space and has no learned sinogram processing, while CTO has a substantial dual-branch sinogram module. Parameter counts and kernel configurations also differ in the primary comparison. Table 11 helps, but does not specify clearly whether its 'identical architecture' variant controls the sinogram branch and every other component, so the large headline gain cannot be cleanly attributed to neural-operator parameterization.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a complex reconstruction study. The abstract's code link is blank; CTO training duration/schedule, random seeds, FFT complex-feature handling, pooling/resampling across arbitrary grids, fan-beam forward/adjoint implementation, complete loss definition, and sufficient hyperparameter-search details are missing. Several supplemental OOD claims provide only averaged gains without full tables or uncertainty.

Baseline fairness is questionable in places. The 65M-parameter diffusion prior is reportedly trained for only 2,000 iterations and evaluated with a costly 1,000-step sampler, making the 'state-of-the-art diffusion' and 500× speed comparisons potentially unrepresentative. The use of scikit-image's parallel-beam iradon_sart baseline is also not reconciled with the stated AAPM fan-beam simulation.

All measurements appear to be retrospectively simulated from reconstructed CT images rather than evaluated on raw clinical projection data. Noise robustness is limited to one simulated Poisson setting, and the AAPM test split appears to contain only one held-out patient. Slice-level means do not account for strong within-patient correlation, and no patient-level confidence intervals or significance tests are reported. These limitations matter given the paper's repeated clinical-practicality framing.

Overall, the approach and numerical results are promising, but the unsupported central generalization and equivariance claims, confounded principal ablation, and incomplete reproducibility leave consequential uncertainty. Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, the current evidence favors a weak reject.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: using one sparse-view CT reconstruction model across multiple acquisition rates and spatial resolutions. The proposed system combines local DISCO operators, an unrolled data-consistency architecture, flipped angular padding, and spatial/frequency sinogram branches into a technically interesting design.

The reported gains are large and consistent across AAPM, KiTS, and LIDC-IDRI, multiple view counts, and several metrics. The paper also includes component ablations, parameter/FLOP comparisons, noise and cross-dataset tests, and inference-time measurements.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly, explains the CT motivation well, and provides useful implementation and baseline details in the supplement.
weaknesses: The central resolution-agnostic claim is not convincingly tested. In the main multi-rate experiment, every model is trained on all four evaluated view counts, so this demonstrates multi-rate co-training rather than generalization to unseen sampling rates. Table 8 likewise trains and tests at the same rates. The only unseen sinogram-resolution test is 72-to-144 views, with no systematic evaluation of interpolation rates, fewer unseen views, shifted angles, nonuniform masks, or scanner geometries.

The key comparison confounds neural-operator parameterization with architecture. The supplement states that the matched Unrolled CNN operates entirely in image space, whereas CTO adds a learned sinogram operator with two branches. Removing the sinogram operator reportedly costs 4.82 dB—larger than much of the CTO-versus-CNN margin. Thus the experiments do not establish that function-space DISCO layers, rather than extra dual-domain processing, cause the main improvements. A matched dual-domain CNN replacing every DISCO layer is essential.

The theoretical geometry does not match the main AAPM experiment. The equivariance proof, flip identity, and Fourier-slice motivation are developed for parallel-beam data over [0,π), but AAPM is simulated using fan-beam geometry over [0,2π). The manuscript does not derive the corresponding fan-beam group action, padding rule, or rebinning procedure. Consequently, the claimed inherent rotation equivariance is unsupported for the primary benchmark.

Rotation equivariance is evaluated only through a 24-view PSNR ablation and qualitative examples. No equivariance error is measured across rotations, and pooling, discretization, interpolation, and nonlinearities may prevent exact equivariance. A performance gain from boundary padding alone does not verify the stronger mathematical claim.

The clinical relevance is overstated. Sinograms are synthetically generated from already reconstructed public CT images, creating an inverse-crime-style setting with matched forward models. There is no evaluation on raw scanner projections, geometry/calibration mismatch, realistic electronic and Poisson noise ranges, or diagnostic/lesion preservation. The single noisy-condition result is reported only as an aggregate gain without absolute scores or comparisons beyond one CNN.

The zero-shot image super-resolution protocol upsamples a 256×256 intermediate reconstruction and compares against a bilinearly upsampled 512×512 target. This target contains no genuine higher-resolution information, making the experiment largely a test of scale consistency rather than super-resolution or recovery of new anatomical detail.

Baseline fairness remains uncertain. CTO's kernel configuration is hyperparameter-tuned, while several baselines are substantially altered from their original single-rate settings; the diffusion prior is reported as trained for only 2,000 iterations despite having 65M parameters. There are no convergence checks, matched tuning budgets, repeated training runs, confidence intervals over seeds, or statistical tests.

Important reproducibility details are missing or ambiguous, including CTO's training duration, complex-valued handling in the FFT branch, exact forward/adjoint implementations and normalization, and full OOD numerical tables. The abstract's code link is blank. Overall, the idea and reported results have merit, but consequential experimental confounds and a geometry-theory mismatch prevent the evidence from supporting the paper's principal claims under the default Algorithms/General assessment.

strengths: This is a relevant Algorithms/General contribution addressing an important practical limitation of learned sparse-view CT: deploying one reconstruction model across acquisition rates and spatial discretizations. The function-space perspective is well motivated and potentially impactful. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/ba55ffbad8924cf3bfa647ad32bc553d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

CTO combines dual-domain processing, physics-based data consistency, localized DISCO kernels, and sinogram spatial/frequency branches in a coherent architecture. The flipped circular padding is a sensible way to encode parallel-beam sinogram boundary structure.

The quantitative results are consistently strong across AAPM, KiTS, and LIDC-IDRI. On AAPM, CTO improves over the unrolled CNN by approximately 2.4–4.5 dB across 18–72 views, while the matched-complexity result still reports a substantial gain. The inference-time advantage over iterative diffusion reconstruction is also practically meaningful.

The evaluation is broader than a single headline table: it includes several view counts, patient-level held-out data, two large test sets, single-rate and multi-rate training, synthetic noise and cross-dataset tests, component ablations, hyperparameter analysis, and computational-cost reporting.

The manuscript is generally clear and well organized, provides useful implementation and baseline-training details, and identifies appropriate future work concerning 3D reconstruction, uncertainty, and broader clinical evaluation.
weaknesses: The most important comparison is confounded. The supplementary material states that the unrolled CNN baseline operates entirely in image space, whereas CTO adds a learned sinogram operator with two branches. Consequently, the reported CTO-versus-CNN gain does not isolate continuous DISCO parameterization from the benefit of additional dual-domain processing. Removing NOs or NOi is not an adequate substitute for replacing each DISCO operator with a standard convolution in an otherwise identical dual-domain architecture. This substantially weakens the central claim that neural operators, rather than the broader architecture, cause the improvement.

The main multi-rate experiments test 9, 18, 36, and 72 views after training on all four rates. They demonstrate that one jointly trained model handles several known settings, but not interpolation or extrapolation to unseen view counts or irregular angular masks. The claim of generalization across sampling rates without retraining is therefore broader than the principal evidence.

The image-space zero-shot super-resolution experiment evaluates against ground truth obtained by bilinearly enlarging a 256×256 image, after also bilinearly enlarging an intermediate reconstruction. This does not test recovery at a genuinely higher native resolution or new high-frequency anatomy. The sinogram-resolution experiment is described mostly through relative gains, without full numerical tables or uncertainty. These issues make the strongest “resolution-agnostic” claim only partially supported.

The rotational-equivariance argument is incomplete for the evaluated system. Flipped circular padding and the proof apply to ideal parallel-beam convolution, while AAPM is simulated with fan-beam geometry, for which the stated p(θ+π,r)=p(θ,−r) relation does not directly apply. Sparse angular masks, pooling, nonlinearities, and discretization can also break exact SO(2) equivariance. A single padding ablation and visual examples at 0°, 90°, and 180° do not quantify equivariance error over arbitrary rotations.

All measurements appear to be synthetically generated from reconstructed CT images using the same forward models used during reconstruction. This inverse-crime-like setup omits raw-projection effects such as scanner calibration, beam hardening, scatter, electronic noise, and geometry mismatch. The one synthetic Poisson-noise experiment reports only average PSNR gains and cannot establish clinical robustness.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the abstract contains an empty code link, and important details such as CTO training duration, preprocessing and normalization, complex-valued handling in the Fourier branch, precise differentiable projector implementation, and complete OOD numerical results are missing. No statistical significance analysis or downstream clinical/task-based evaluation is supplied. Overall, the idea and empirical results favor acceptance, but the architectural confound and incomplete validation of the core generalization claims keep the recommendation borderline.
